planting.note: Direct sow in hills once soil has thoroughly warmed past last frost; Anne Arundel is a colonial-era Maryland heirloom muskmelon needing a full warm season to size and sweeten its fruit.

directions: Anne Arundel is a colonial Maryland heirloom traced to Anne Arundel County, where it was grown by a small circle of local farmers for well over a century. Its nutmeg-shaped fruit ripens to a golden-yellow rind over sweet, pale green flesh with a flavor often compared to honeydew. The strain nearly vanished before being preserved through much of the twentieth century by a Maryland family, and it now circulates through Seed Savers Exchange membership. Give vines full sun and steady moisture through fruit set, then ease off watering as melons approach ripeness to concentrate their sweetness.

planting.note: Direct sow after soil warms; bred for extremely short seasons, Far North can also be started indoors a couple weeks early in very cool climates to guarantee a harvest.

directions: Far North is a compact, extra-early heirloom muskmelon bred specifically for gardeners in short-season and far-northern climates, ripening its small, lightly netted fruit in as little as two months from direct seeding. It trades the larger fruit size and richer sugars of long-season eastern cantaloupes for the reliability of actually finishing before fall frost arrives, making it a practical fallback where standard cantaloupe varieties routinely fail to ripen. Vines stay relatively compact compared with vigorous heirloom types, so they fit reasonably well in smaller garden beds. Today the variety is kept in circulation mainly through small regional seed-preservation growers rather than mainstream catalogs.

planting.note: Direct sow once soil is warm; this ultra-early variety was bred for high-altitude and short-season regions where standard cantaloupes cannot ripen in time.

directions: Montana Gold was originally offered as an ultra-early cantaloupe for gardeners coping with high elevation and short, cool growing seasons. Its compact vines set small fruit with notably thick, sweet flesh, ripening well ahead of the 85-90 day eastern cantaloupe standards most catalogs offer. It remains a practical choice anywhere summers run too short or too cool for full-season melons, though its fruit size and yield are modest compared with longer-season heirlooms. The variety persists today mainly through small regional seed-saving networks rather than large commercial suppliers.

planting.note: Direct sow or transplant once soil is reliably warm; Vedrantais rewards a hot, dry finish that concentrates its intensely perfumed flesh.

directions: Vedrantais is a classic, open-pollinated French Charentais heirloom that many chefs and growers regard as the truest expression of the Charentais type, distinct from generic Charentais seed blends sold under that name alone. Fruit is small and round with a smooth, gray-green rind lightly ribbed toward the blossom end, enclosing deep-orange flesh with an intensely honeyed, floral aroma prized in French markets. Because Charentais types slip cleanly from the vine only at full ripeness, check plants daily as harvest approaches and watch for a faint crack or softening at the stem end rather than waiting for the fruit to fall free on its own. A hot, relatively dry growing season brings out the fullest sugar and fragrance this variety is known for.

planting.note: Direct sow once soil has warmed; Sweet Granite was bred specifically for far-northern, coastal, and mountain gardens with short cantaloupe seasons.

directions: Sweet Granite was released by a University of New Hampshire plant breeding program as one of the earliest-ripening eastern-type cantaloupes available at the time, developed specifically for gardeners in short-season northern, coastal, and mountain climates. The oblong fruit carries light netting over sweet, orange flesh and averages about three pounds, smaller than many long-season commercial cantaloupes but far more reliable where summers run cool or short. It remains a dependable option today for gardeners north of the traditional cantaloupe belt who still want genuine muskmelon flavor. Give it full sun and consistent moisture through fruit set, tapering off as melons approach full slip.
sources: University of New Hampshire Cooperative Extension

planting.note: Direct sow once soil is warm; Oka was bred for Quebec's short, cool season and performs best in a warm microclimate at more northern latitudes.

directions: Oka was bred in the early twentieth century at the Trappist monastery of Oka, Quebec, as a deliberate cross of the Montreal Melon and the Banana Melon, aimed at combining rich flavor with a shorter season than the giant Montreal type required. It produces small, flattened, roughly ten-ribbed fruit with aromatic, sweet orange flesh well suited to Quebec's cool summers. It fell out of wide commercial circulation by mid-century as industrial melon varieties took over, only to be rediscovered decades later from seed preserved near Montreal. It is grown today largely through Quebec heirloom seed farms working to keep the revival going.

common_name: Feher Ozon Paprika Pepper (Hungarian Heirloom Sweet Paprika)

planting.note: Start indoors 8-10 weeks before last frost; Feher Ozon is a Hungarian heirloom paprika pepper grown for drying and grinding into homemade sweet paprika.

directions: Feher Ozon is a Hungarian heirloom whose name translates roughly to 'white torrent,' referring to the ivory-white color of its immature pods before they ripen through orange to red. Compact, upright plants stay productive under garden conditions and set heavy clusters of thick-walled, tapering pods around five inches long, with a mild, fruity sweetness and essentially no heat. It belongs to the classic family of Hungarian paprika peppers grown specifically to be dried and ground into homemade sweet paprika, though the fresh pods are equally good sliced raw, roasted, or stuffed. Its dwarf, self-supporting habit makes it easier to manage in small gardens than taller Hungarian paprika types.

planting.note: Start indoors 8-10 weeks before last frost; Friariello grows tall and heavy with fruit, so stake or cage plants to prevent breakage.

directions: Friariello is a traditional Neapolitan frying pepper whose name derives from the Italian verb for frying, reflecting centuries of use in southern Italian home kitchens. Tall, vigorous plants bear small, tri-lobed, thin-walled pods only a few inches long that mature from green to bright red, with a sweet flavor and no measurable heat. The classic preparation fries the whole pepper, seeds and skin included, in olive oil with garlic until blistered, then finishes it with tomato and fresh basil. Because the plants grow taller and set a heavier fruit load than many bell-type sweet peppers, staking or caging helps keep the brittle branches from snapping under the weight.

common_name: Peperone di Senise (Basilicata Sweet Drying Pepper)

planting.note: Start indoors 8-10 weeks before last frost; traditionally grown in the hot, dry summers of Basilicata and best suited to a long, warm season for full drying.

directions: Peperone di Senise takes its name from the town of Senise in the Basilicata region of southern Italy, where farmers have long selected this thin-fleshed sweet pepper and it now carries a protected geographical indication. Pods are elongated and tapering, hooked or twisted depending on the strain, and their unusually thin flesh dries quickly on strings hung in the sun without rotting. Once fully dried, the pods are known as peperoni cruschi, deep-fried briefly until shatteringly crisp and used as a garnish or snack throughout Basilicata, or ground into a red seasoning. Because the whole point of the variety is easy sun-drying, it performs best where summers are long, hot, and relatively dry.

common_name: Kurtovska Kapia Pepper (Bulgarian Heirloom Sweet Pepper)

planting.note: Start indoors 8-10 weeks before last frost; a traditional field variety from the Plovdiv region of Bulgaria, grown for both fresh eating and preserving.

directions: Kurtovska Kapia is a traditional Bulgarian heirloom sweet pepper from the Plovdiv area of central southern Bulgaria, recognized on Slow Food's Ark of Taste as a distinctive regional food. Plants stay relatively low and bushy but produce heavy, hanging clusters of large, flattened, heart-shaped pods that ripen from dark green to deep red with tender, juicy, notably sweet flesh. Its broad, meaty shoulders and pointed tip typify the wider kapia class of Balkan and Turkish sweet peppers used fresh, roasted, or preserved into spreads such as lutenitsa and ajvar. Because fruit is often left to fully redden before harvest for maximum sweetness, this variety benefits from a long, warm growing season.
